newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour say government disintegrating over EU.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour say government disintegrating over EU.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party launched a fresh attack on Prime Minister John Major on Wednesday, saying the latest government split over Europe showed his administration was disintegrating.

Major's Conservatives, seeking a fifth consecutive term in the May 1 election, were rocked when two junior health ministers flouted government policy by declaring their opposition to Britain joining a single European currency.

"This is the legacy of six years of weak leadership which leads to a situation where you've got a government literally in the middle of an election campaign virtually disintegrating before our eyes," Labour leader Tony Blair told BBC radio.

"Now he's faced with a position where ministers aren't holding to the line and he simply caves in again. Now you can't run a party like that and you certainly can't run a government like that," he said.

Major, who has long been battling to stop his party splitting over policy towards the European Union, made clear last month that ministers should stick to his "wait and see" policy over a possible single European currency.
But late on Tuesday junior health minister John Horam reopened old wounds by issuing an election manifesto which made it clear he was against the idea.

"I personally am opposed to a single currency but I think the right line is to stay at the negotiating table...and wait and see what happens," Horam said in a television interview, denying that he was out of line with government policy.
James Paice, a junior education minister, was also at odds with the government in his election address, saying a single currency would lead to political union.

Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind denied on Wednesday that Horam had strayed from government policy, saying the junior minister had made "a perfectly reasonable statement fully in line with government policy".
But Blair said it was clear to all that the Conservatives were a spent political force.

"How on earth do they go to Europe and get a good deal for Britain if they can't even hold their own government together? How do they represent British national interests properly in those circumstances?" he said.
Major's party took a further blow when The Times newspaper said a further nine ministers, including two in cabinet posts, were breaching the government line in private.

The Conservatives, trailing by up to 21 points in the latest opinion polls, had hoped that the tide was turning for them and that good news would be on the way in the shape of a string of economic figures out on Wednesday.
The jobless figures are expected to show 45,000 more people left the dole queues in March. Unemployment is at a six-year low after dropping consistently over the last 30 months.
But newspapers said the government had admitted understating the number of jobless in an application for funds submitted to the European Commission.

The Mirror, which had leaked the figures for the past two months, said the official jobless number was expected to be 1,700,000 but in reality it was much higher, perhaps as high as four to five million.
